claims.claim: StoryScope measured narrators explicitly explaining the story's theme in 77% of AI stories versus 52% of human stories.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: Narrators explicitly explain the story’s theme 77% of the time

claims.claim: StoryScope characterises the AI pattern as over-determination in which the model spells out meaning rather than trusting the reader to infer it.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: AI spells out meaning rather than trusting the reader to infer it

claims.claim: StoryScope measured AI dialogue serving philosophical debate in 59% of AI stories against 34% of human stories.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: AI dialogue serves philosophical debate more often (59% vs. 34%)

claims.claim: StoryScope measured 79% of AI stories carrying no subplots against 57% of human stories.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6

claims.claim: StoryScope measured AI stories conveying emotion through physical sensations and bodily metaphors in 81% of cases against 38% for humans, so on this corpus the AI writing is the more bodily-concrete of the two.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: conveys emotion through physical sensations and bodily metaphors (81% vs. 38% human)

claims.claim: StoryScope measured human authors using explicit emotion labels 29% of the time against 8% for AI.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: Humans use explicit emotion labels 29% of the time versus just 8%

claims.claim: StoryScope measured smell-based imagery in 82% of AI stories against 57% of human stories.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6

claims.claim: StoryScope measured humans referencing specific texts and authors at 47% against 24% for AI, which sticks to vague allusions and avoids naming real brands, places or works.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: Humans reference specific texts and authors at nearly double the AI rate

claims.claim: StoryScope measured direct address to the reader in 28% of human stories against 7% of AI stories.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: address the reader directly more frequently (28% vs. 7%)

claims.claim: StoryScope reports that discourse-level narrative features alone reach 93.2% macro-F1 at human-versus-AI detection, without any stylistic signal.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6

claims.claim: After span-level rewriting that removes surface AI artifacts such as cliche and purple prose, StoryScope's narrative classifier lost only 1.6 macro-F1 points on edited Gemini stories.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6

claims.claim: StoryScope measured 24.7% of human stories falling in the corpus-wide rarest ten per cent of narrative-feature space against 7.1% of AI stories.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.page: rarity analysis, mean Euclidean distance to 25 nearest neighbours

claims.claim: StoryScope's human comparison corpus is 10,272 short stories extracted from Books3, so its register is published literary fiction and not any archival or record register.
claims.source: Russell, Rajendhran, Pham, Iyyer and Wieting, StoryScope, arXiv:2604.03136v6
claims.quote: We extract 10,272 human-written stories from Books3

claims.feature: other: continuity across a long text

claims.quote: It also isn’t good at sustaining anything with continuity.
claims.page: 'two key problems with Gen AI in writing', problem 1

claims.feature: other: surface polish with nothing underneath
claims.claim: Wendig asserts that generative AI is not there to get things right but to make things look right.
claims.quote: it’s here to make things look right

verdicts.trueWording: Narrators explicitly explain the story's theme 77% of the time, versus 52%
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML (curl, 459KB) §4.1 'AI over-explains its themes': quote exact; both figures and the AI/human assignment match.

verdicts.trueWording: The pattern is one of over-determination: AI spells out meaning
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §4.1: 'The pattern is one of over-determination: AI spells out meaning rather than trusting the reader to infer it.' Quote exact; the over-determination framing is the page's own word.

verdicts.trueWording: AI dialogue serves philosophical debate more often (59% vs. 34%)
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §4.1, same paragraph as the 77%/52% sentence. Quote exact; 59% AI / 34% human confirmed.
Raw arXiv HTML §4.1 'Human authors subvert linearity'. Quote exact including the curly quotes; 79% AI / 57% human confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: AI overwhelmingly conveys emotion through physical sensations and bodily metaphors
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §4.1 'AI over-writes the body and senses'. Quote exact. The counter-evidence limb is the page's own reading: heading plus 'AI renders fear as a tightening chest, cold sweat' vs humans naming feelings.

verdicts.trueWording: Humans use explicit emotion labels 29% of the time versus just 8% for AI
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §4.1, closing sentence of the body/senses paragraph. Quote exact; direction (humans higher) confirmed.
Raw arXiv HTML §4.1. Quote exact; the 82% is AI, 57% human, matching the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: Humans reference specific texts and authors at nearly double the AI rate (47% vs. 24%)
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §4.1 'Human authors engage the outside world'. Quote exact; the second limb is near-verbatim on the page: 'AI generally sticks to vague allusions and avoids naming real brands, places, or works.'

verdicts.trueWording: address the reader directly more frequently (28% vs. 7%)
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §4.1. Quote exact; 28% human / 7% AI confirmed by the sentence subject ('Humans break the fourth wall far more often... and address the reader').

verdicts.trueWording: Narrative features alone achieve 93.2% macro-F1 for human vs. AI detection
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML abstract, quote exact. 'Discourse-level' is the paper's own gloss (§1: 'Discourse-level narrative features ... which we refer to simply as narrative features throughout'); 'without any stylistic signal' matches §4 'withholding all stylistic features'.

verdicts.trueWording: 93.9% macro-F1 edited vs 95.5% original, a drop of only 1.6 points
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §4.2 'Surface editing barely affects narrative detection'. Quote exact. Every limb holds: LAMP is Chakrabarty et al. (2025)'s span-level rewriting framework, its artifact categories include cliché and purple prose, and it was applied to 278 Gemini-generated stories.

verdicts.trueWording: 24.7% of all human stories fall in the top 10% rarest corpus-wide, vs 7.1% of AI
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML rarity analysis. Quote fragment '24.7% of all human' exact (the sentence wraps a line). Rarity is defined there as mean Euclidean distance to a story's 25 nearest neighbours in narrative feature space, matching the claim's page hint.

verdicts.trueWording: We extract 10,272 human-written stories from Books3, from short story anthologies
verdicts.note: Raw arXiv HTML §3 'Data.': quote exact, and 'human-written short stories' plus 'we identify and extract stories from short story anthologies identified via running Gemini 2.5 Flash over titles and blurbs in Books3' supports the corpus limb. But the paper never characterises the corpus's register: it says nothing about 'literary fiction' (grep for 'literary fiction'/'genre' returns nothing descriptive of the human corpus, only Table 4's word-count summary), and makes no contrast with archival or record registers. That inference is the claim author's, not the page's.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the corpus register is published literary fiction and not an archival or record register

verdicts.trueWording: It also isn't good at sustaining anything with continuity
